1. The frames show a row of houses with one dark house in the middle, labeled "June 2006." The dark house is the "darkest house," meaning the worst starting point for a buyer. The top banner says the data come from FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac rates. It also says "ILLUSTRATIVE," "US only," and "history, not a forecast." The idea is that someone who bought at the June 2006 peak ended up far worse off than a renter would have.

2. Not much changes across the six frames. The title "The darkest house" in frames 1–2 becomes "$82,385 behind" in frames 3–6. The houses on either side shift slightly, with some lighter and some darker, and the dark house stays dark. The date stays at June 2006.

3. The label suggests that a buyer in June 2006 ended up $82,385 behind a renter who put the same money elsewhere. This is after counting the costs of owning, such as interest, taxes, insurance and repairs. The animation doesn't say how long the comparison runs, so I can't tell the end date. The lighter houses suggest that buyers at other times fared better.

4. A viewer would probably conclude that when you buy matters a lot. Buying at a market peak can leave you worse off than renting, and buying isn't automatically better than renting. The caveats about history and the US suggest the viewer shouldn't treat one past result as a prediction.

5. The animation only partly suggests this. The "$82,385 behind" figure, the "darkest house" label and the "history, not a forecast" caveat are on screen. No on-screen text gives advice such as "rent" or "wait to buy." The advice in point 4 is my own conclusion. The animation also doesn't show what the $82,385 is measured against, so my reading of "behind a renter" is an inference from the frames.
